paragraphs: SimCLR studies how to learn useful image representations without labels through contrastive learning. Its framework avoids specialized network architectures and a memory bank, making the learning setup simpler. The paper’s central contribution is a systematic examination of which components make the contrastive prediction task produce representations that work well for subsequent classification.

Three findings guide the design. Combining data augmentations appropriately is critical because these transformations define the prediction task. A learned nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves representation quality. The experiments also find that contrastive learning benefits from larger batches and more training steps compared with supervised learning.

Together, these choices produce strong ImageNet results. A linear classifier on the learned representations reaches 76.5% top-1 accuracy, matching a supervised ResNet-50 and improving relatively by 7% over the previous state of the art. Fine-tuning with only 1% of labels reaches 85.8% top-5 accuracy. These evaluations show that the learned features support both direct classification and adaptation with limited labels.
icml-2020-a-simple-framework-for-contras.tldr: SimCLR shows how augmentation, a nonlinear transformation, and training scale combine to produce strong image representations without labels.

paragraphs: This paper addresses optimization when gradients are unavailable, so an algorithm must work through function evaluations. It focuses on objectives expressed as a finite sum of component functions. That structure offers information an optimizer can exploit, but existing stochastic methods in this setting had not been theoretically shown to achieve an accelerated convergence rate.

The authors design a derivative-free algorithm that uses the finite-sum structure to reduce variance. This matters because attempts to accelerate stochastic derivative-free methods can become unstable and struggle to converge. The proposed approach connects acceleration with control of the variability arising in the optimization process, rather than treating speed alone as the design goal.

The paper proves convergence rates for smooth convex objectives and for strongly convex objectives with finite-sum structure. These results establish acceleration within those stated problem classes. Experiments across several tasks and datasets support the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore both an algorithm and a justification that acceleration can be achieved in this gradient-unavailable setting.
icml-2020-an-accelerated-dfo-algorithm-f.tldr: A variance-reduced derivative-free algorithm provably accelerates optimization of smooth convex and strongly convex finite-sum objectives.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence can be a poor guide to how difficult an image really is. Convolutional networks may be highly confident even when an example is ambiguous. This paper proposes angular visual hardness, or AVH, to assess difficulty using the normalized angle between an example’s feature representation and its target classifier.

The study finds that networks with the highest classification accuracy also have the best AVH scores, consistent with earlier evidence that stronger models improve on difficult examples. AVH also behaves differently from the training loss: it quickly levels off across samples while the loss continues to decrease. The authors interpret this difference as motivation for losses that address harder examples more effectively.

AVH has a statistically significant correlation with human judgments of visual difficulty. This supports its relevance as a measure of hardness, without making it interchangeable with human perception. The paper also demonstrates benefits in self-training for domain adaptation and in domain generalization, connecting the proposed score to practical learning applications.
icml-2020-angular-visual-hardness-db9272.tldr: Angular visual hardness measures image difficulty through feature angles and reveals behavior that training loss and model confidence can miss.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures dependence between variables, and some learning problems seek to reduce it. Doing so is difficult in high-dimensional settings, especially when only samples are available and the underlying distributions are unknown. The paper addresses a mismatch in existing approaches: much previous work estimates lower bounds, which do not provide the needed basis for minimizing mutual information.

The authors introduce CLUB, a contrastive log-ratio upper bound. An upper bound provides a quantity that can be optimized to control mutual information from above. They analyze the bound and its variational approximation, then build a training procedure for mutual-information minimization. A negative-sampling strategy accelerates that procedure.

Experiments with Gaussian distributions support CLUB’s ability to estimate mutual information reliably in the studied simulations. Applications to domain adaptation and the information bottleneck demonstrate its effectiveness in practical minimization tasks. The contribution connects a theoretically analyzed bound with a usable training method, targeting the direction of optimization that lower-bound approaches do not directly address.
icml-2020-club-a-contrastive-log-ratio-u.tldr: CLUB introduces a mutual-information upper bound and an accelerated training procedure for reducing dependence between learned variables.

paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to learning from graphs: kernel methods and graph convolutional neural networks. It introduces multilayer graph kernels by extending convolutional kernel networks to graph-structured inputs. A graph is represented through successive kernel feature maps, with each node carrying information about local structures in the graph.

The connection offers two ways to use the model. From the kernel perspective, it supplies an expressive representation that can be learned without supervision and is straightforward to regularize. The authors emphasize its usefulness when training samples are limited. The same framework can also be trained end-to-end on large datasets, yielding new forms of graph convolutional networks.

On several graph classification benchmarks, the method achieves competitive performance and offers simple model interpretation. These findings support the value of a common framework that accommodates both unsupervised representations and end-to-end learning. Its significance lies in linking local graph structure, kernel representations, and neural training within one family of models, rather than requiring a separate construction for each approach.
icml-2020-convolutional-kernel-networks-.tldr: Multilayer graph kernels connect interpretable, unsupervised graph representations with graph neural networks that can also train end-to-end.

paragraphs: Embedding layers assign continuous vectors to discrete symbols so that a model can represent their meanings numerically. Their storage cost grows linearly with the number of symbols. Consequently, even an effective embedding layer can become a major obstacle when a system has limited memory or storage capacity.

The paper introduces differentiable product quantization, or DPQ, as a general framework for compressing embeddings while learning them end-to-end. It presents two versions that use different approximation techniques to make the compression compatible with differentiable training. The framework is designed to replace an existing embedding layer directly, making compression part of the model’s learning process.

Across ten datasets covering three language tasks, DPQ achieves compression ratios ranging from 14 to 238 times with negligible or no observed performance loss. These results indicate that substantial embedding compression can coexist with useful task performance in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is an adaptable compression framework whose representations can be optimized together with the rest of the model.
icml-2020-differentiable-product-quantiz.tldr: DPQ makes embedding compression trainable end-to-end, achieving 14–238-fold compression with negligible or no performance cost in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Randomized Newton methods make large-scale and distributed optimization more manageable by replacing expensive calculations with randomized approximations. This creates a trade-off: computation becomes cheaper, but the resulting solution contains approximation error. The practical difficulty is that users often do not know how large that error is for the solution they actually obtain.

The paper explains why two common ways of managing this uncertainty can be unsatisfactory. Worst-case theoretical bounds may contain unknown constants and can encourage unnecessary computation. Alternatively, choosing the sketch size and stopping rule through heuristics can leave the quality of a result uncertain. Both difficulties arise from lacking a direct assessment of the approximation error.

The authors show how bootstrapping can estimate that unknown error directly. This gives users a more concrete basis for judging the quality of a randomized solution and avoiding excessive computation. The contribution concerns the reliability of the computation-accuracy trade-off itself: estimating the error helps make the computational savings of randomized optimization more usable.
icml-2020-estimating-the-error-of-random.tldr: Bootstrapping estimates randomized Newton methods’ approximation error directly, helping users assess solution quality without unnecessary computation.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether the generative pretraining approach used for language can also learn useful image representations. The authors train a sequence Transformer to predict pixels autoregressively, without explicitly building the image’s two-dimensional structure into the model. Training uses low-resolution ImageNet images without labels and a model at GPT-2 scale.

The learned representations are evaluated through linear probing, full fine-tuning, and classification with limited data. These evaluations examine whether features learned from pixel prediction can support recognition tasks. The paper finds strong results, showing that a sequential generative objective can learn image information useful beyond the pixel-prediction task itself.

On CIFAR-10, a linear probe reaches 96.3% accuracy, exceeding a supervised Wide ResNet, while full fine-tuning reaches 99.0%, matching the leading supervised pretrained models in the comparison. A configuration using a VQVAE encoding achieves 69.0% top-1 linear-probe accuracy on ImageNet and is competitive with self-supervised benchmarks. Together, the results support generative pretraining as a route to useful visual features.
icml-2020-generative-pretraining-from-pi.tldr: A sequence Transformer trained to predict image pixels without labels learns representations that support strong image classification results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a high-dimensional mean when a constant fraction of the observations are adversarial outliers. Earlier work had developed sophisticated polynomial-time algorithms with error guarantees independent of dimension for several natural distribution families. The question here is whether a more direct optimization approach can address this robust estimation problem.

The authors show that gradient descent can solve a natural nonconvex formulation. Their central structural result says, roughly, that any approximate stationary point of the objective yields a near-optimal robust estimate. A stationary point is a place where the optimization has little local direction for improvement, so connecting such points to estimation quality is crucial.

This connection explains why reaching approximate stationarity can be enough for the underlying statistical task in the analyzed formulation. It provides a bridge between high-dimensional robust statistics and nonconvex optimization, with gradient descent serving as the algorithmic link. The authors suggest that the connection may extend to other robust estimation problems, while presenting that broader applicability as a possibility.
icml-2020-high-dimensional-robust-mean-e.tldr: A structural result makes gradient descent sufficient to obtain near-optimal robust mean estimates from a natural nonconvex formulation.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models can help measure similarity by representing data in a smaller space. However, ordinary Euclidean distance in that space ignores similarity information contained in the decoder. This paper modifies variational autoencoders so that simple distances in the learned latent space better reflect the geometry associated with decoded data.

The authors describe latent space as a Riemannian manifold and regularize its metric tensor toward a scaled identity matrix. In plain terms, they encourage a geometry in which distance behaves uniformly enough for Euclidean measurements to serve as a useful proxy. They also introduce a more expressive hierarchical prior and formulate training as constrained optimization.

The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including a video-tracking benchmark. On that benchmark, the unsupervised approach approaches the performance of leading supervised methods while keeping the computational efficiency of approaches based on straight lines. The result illustrates the motivation for learning a flatter geometry: incorporating decoder-informed similarity can remain compatible with inexpensive distance calculations.
icml-2020-learning-flat-latent-manifolds.tldr: A modified variational autoencoder learns flatter latent geometry so efficient Euclidean distances can better represent data similarity.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can depend on both the individual example and its true label. This makes label noise more complicated than a single uniform corruption rate. The paper studies a bounded version of this setting, where the probabilities of labels being flipped have an upper bound strictly below one.

The authors introduce distilled examples: examples whose labels agree with the labels assigned by the Bayes optimal classifier. This definition ties the useful training examples to the best classification decision under the underlying distribution. They prove that, under certain conditions, classifiers trained on distilled examples converge to that optimal classifier.

The distilled-example idea then motivates an algorithm with theoretical guarantees of robustness to the bounded noise setting. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The significance is the connection between a precisely defined kind of trustworthy example and a learning procedure for corrupted labels. Both the bounded-noise assumption and the conditions behind the convergence result are part of the stated theoretical scope.
icml-2020-learning-with-bounded-instance.tldr: Distilled examples motivate a theoretically supported algorithm for learning when label corruption depends on the example and label but remains bounded.

paragraphs: Combinatorial semi-bandits extend classic bandit learning to decisions involving multiple base arms and richer feedback. Protecting that feedback with differential privacy can introduce an additional dependence on data dimension. This paper asks whether that extra dimensional burden is unavoidable under central differential privacy and the stronger local differential privacy setting.

Under two common smoothness assumptions, the authors show how to avoid the additional dimension-related penalty. For B-infinity-bounded smooth problems, they give algorithms and matching lower bounds for both privacy settings. The local-private rate depends inversely on the square of the privacy parameter, whereas the central-private rate depends inversely on the parameter itself, up to the stated logarithmic qualifications.

For B-one-bounded smooth problems under central privacy, the optimal rate also includes the maximum amount of feedback per round. Across these cases, the bounds nearly match the corresponding non-private optimal rates in the sense described by the paper. The result concerns removing an extra dimensional cost under the specified assumptions; the bounds still explicitly capture dependence on privacy strength.
icml-2020-locally-differentially-private.tldr: Under specified smoothness assumptions, private combinatorial semi-bandits achieve optimal regret bounds without an additional dimension-related privacy penalty.

paragraphs: Turning a problem written in natural language into a formal program requires recovering symbolic relationships that may only be implicit in the wording. General neural sequence models do not explicitly represent this structure. The paper proposes TP-N2F, an encoder-decoder model that makes structured representations central to both understanding the input and constructing the output.

The model uses Tensor Product Representations. Its encoder applies binding to represent symbolic structure in vector space. Its decoder applies unbinding to generate a program as a sequence of relational tuples, each containing an operation or relation and its arguments. This supplies an explicit structural connection between the language representation and the formal solution.

On two benchmarks, TP-N2F considerably outperforms LSTM-based sequence-to-sequence models and establishes new leading results. Ablation studies attribute the improvements to using structured representations in both encoder and decoder. Analysis of the learned structures also shows improved interpretability. The findings support explicitly representing symbolic organization when the required output must itself follow a formal relational structure.
icml-2020-mapping-natural-language-probl.tldr: TP-N2F uses structured tensor representations to translate natural-language problems into formal programs more accurately and interpretably.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to protect models against small input perturbations that can cause prediction errors. It can also increase generalization error on unperturbed test data relative to standard training. This paper examines the common expectation that collecting more training data should reduce that clean-test performance gap.

The authors analyze robust classifiers in Gaussian and Bernoulli models under attacks constrained by the infinity norm. They prove that additional training data can increase the gap between robust and standard models. This is a statement about their relative generalization errors: a larger gap does not by itself establish that both models, or either individual model, become worse with more data.

The theory also identifies whether and when further data will begin reducing the gap. Experiments demonstrate the phenomenon for linear regression as well, suggesting that it may extend beyond the classification settings analyzed theoretically. The findings make the role of sample size more nuanced: more data can change the robust-versus-standard comparison in different directions depending on the setting.
icml-2020-more-data-can-expand-the-gener.tldr: More training data can widen the clean-test generalization gap between robust and standard models in the settings analyzed.

paragraphs: Transfer learning commonly starts with designated source and target domains. This paper instead considers many heterogeneous domains, each of which might be a target of interest or provide useful information to another domain. The problem becomes identifying which domains can help one another, rather than assuming their transfer roles are already known.

The method relies on mutual learnability: datasets must be similar enough to be regarded as coming from the same population to serve as useful sources for one another. Under this assumption, the authors propose confidence distribution fusion to recover the relationships that determine where information can be shared. The aim is selective transfer across the collection of domains.

The proposed method achieves the same oracle statistical inference accuracy as if the true learnability structure were known. It also supports efficient parallel implementation for large-scale data. Simulated and real examples illustrate its usefulness. The result links discovering suitable transfer partners with preserving inference quality, while grounding that guarantee in the stated mutual learnability assumption.
icml-2020-mutual-transfer-learning-for-m.tldr: Mutual transfer learning identifies compatible domains for sharing information and achieves oracle inference accuracy under a mutual learnability assumption.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses labeled and unlabeled data together. This paper introduces NS3L, a method motivated by negative sampling and contrastive estimation. The authors describe it as simple, fast, and easy to tune, and investigate its usefulness as an additional loss within existing semi-supervised learning algorithms.

Adding the NS3L loss to Virtual Adversarial Training produces significant improvements over both ordinary VAT and its variant with entropy minimization. The authors also add the loss to MixMatch and observe significant gains over the original method. These comparisons test whether NS3L contributes useful learning information when combined with already strong approaches.

The experimental study covers CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, and STL10, and includes an ablation study of hyperparameter tuning. The stated findings support NS3L as a useful addition across the evaluated semi-supervised methods and benchmarks. Its practical contribution is a loss that can improve established learning procedures, with experiments examining both the resulting performance and the role of its tuning choices.
icml-2020-negative-sampling-in-semi-supe.tldr: NS3L adds a negative-sampling-inspired loss that significantly improves VAT and MixMatch in the reported semi-supervised learning experiments.

paragraphs: Some adversarial defenses make predictions by inverting a deep generative model rather than using only a straightforward forward computation. That inversion can obscure the gradients needed by an attack. This paper investigates how to attack such defenses when the attacker has white-box access to the model and its computation.

The proposed attack treats inversion as a dynamical system. It backtracks through the system’s trajectory to extract a gradient with respect to the input image. This directly addresses the computational process responsible for obscuring the gradient. The authors also develop an amortized strategy to accelerate the attack, making the proposed approach more efficient.

Experiments show that the attack breaks defenses including DefenseGAN and ABS more effectively than comparison attacks such as BPDA. The empirical analysis also provides insight into weaknesses of generative-model defenses. The contribution is an evaluation method that accounts for the inversion procedure itself, demonstrating that difficulty obtaining a useful gradient can conceal vulnerabilities in the defenses studied.
icml-2020-on-breaking-deep-generative-mo.tldr: A white-box attack traces generative-model inversion dynamics to recover useful gradients and more effectively break the evaluated defenses.

paragraphs: Checkpoints preserve model states that are useful for training and diagnosis, but storing and recovering them can be expensive. This paper introduces LC-Checkpoint, a lossy compression method designed to improve both checkpoint compactness and recovery speed. Its design explicitly assumes that the model is trained using stochastic gradient descent.

LC-Checkpoint combines quantization with priority promotion to retain information that is most important for SGD recovery. It then applies Huffman coding to exploit the uneven distribution of gradient scales. These components connect the storage representation to the recovery process, so the method considers what training needs after a checkpoint is restored.

The experiments report compression of up to 28 times and recovery speedups of up to 5.77 times over SCAR, the comparison method. These are reported maxima, rather than uniform gains for every checkpoint. The findings demonstrate that a checkpoint scheme tailored to SGD can improve both storage efficiency and recovery performance, with lossy storage forming an explicit part of the approach.
icml-2020-on-efficient-constructions-of-.tldr: LC-Checkpoint uses SGD-aware lossy compression to reduce checkpoint storage and accelerate recovery in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a function’s values accurately does not necessarily provide enough information to optimize it. For maximum coverage, earlier results ruled out constant-factor approximation from polynomially many independent samples containing only a set and its value. This difficulty can remain even when most function values can be approximately learned with high probability.

The paper proposes optimization from structured samples, a stronger model in which observations also reveal structural information about the coverage function. Under three assumptions on the sampling distributions, the authors construct efficient algorithms that achieve constant-factor approximations. The change in what the samples reveal makes a provable optimization guarantee possible.

The authors also establish a constant lower bound that is tight when computational efficiency is set aside. Removing any one of the three distributional assumptions eliminates the constant-approximation guarantee in this model. These results identify both the value and the limits of structured observations: useful optimization depends on the information samples contain and on the conditions governing how those samples are obtained.
icml-2020-optimization-from-structured-s.tldr: Structural information in samples enables constant-factor maximum-coverage approximation under three assumptions that are essential to the stated guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper seeks compact representations of sequential data that preserve useful spatial and temporal information. It frames the task as contrastive representation learning and introduces an objective based on optimal transport. The goal is to learn a low-dimensional subspace that retains informative properties of the original sequence.

The objective combines three requirements: separate the embedded data from an adversarial distribution using Wasserstein distance, preserve temporal order, and reduce distortion of the data. To construct the adversarial distribution, the authors connect a Wasserstein GAN with a classifier. This provides a mechanism for producing negative distributions, addressing an important difficulty in defining contrastive learning tasks.

The full formulation becomes a subspace-learning problem on the Grassmann manifold and is solved with Riemannian optimization. Experiments on human action recognition in video sequences show competitive performance against challenging baselines. The findings support combining distributional separation with explicit attention to sequence order and representation fidelity when learning compact features for this task.
icml-2020-representation-learning-via-ad.tldr: An optimal-transport contrastive objective learns compact sequence representations by combining adversarial separation, temporal order, and low distortion.

paragraphs: Retrosynthetic planning works backward from a desired product to identify reactions that could produce it. The number of possible transformations creates a large search space, making route planning difficult even for experienced chemists. Existing approaches can require costly, high-variance rollout estimates or emphasize search speed at the expense of route quality.

Retro* combines an A*-like search procedure with learned neural guidance. It organizes the search as an AND-OR tree and learns a search bias from off-policy data. During a new planning episode, the neural network guides best-first search, helping the algorithm decide which possibilities to explore as it constructs a route.

On USPTO benchmark datasets, the method improves success rate and solution quality over existing leading approaches while also being more efficient. These findings support combining learned guidance with structured search to address route quality and computational effort together. The reported contribution is an efficient method for finding high-quality synthetic routes, supported by benchmark comparisons on all three aspects.
icml-2020-retro-learning-retrosynthetic-.tldr: Retro* uses neural guidance within an A*-like search to find better synthetic routes more efficiently on USPTO benchmarks.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks learn from graph-structured data, but adding layers can cause over-smoothing: node representations become too similar to remain useful. This helps explain why many successful graph convolutional models are shallow. The paper studies how to design deeper networks while relieving this obstacle.

The authors propose GCNII, an extension of the standard graph convolutional network with two techniques: initial residual and identity mapping. These modifications form the core of the architecture. The paper provides both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence that together they effectively reduce the over-smoothing problem, giving support for using greater depth.

Experiments show that deep GCNII models outperform leading methods on a variety of semi-supervised and fully supervised tasks. The results connect the architectural changes to improved predictive performance in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a relatively simple route to deeper graph convolutional models, with analysis explaining why the added techniques help and experiments showing that the resulting depth can be useful.
icml-2020-simple-and-deep-graph-convolut.tldr: GCNII uses initial residual and identity mapping to relieve over-smoothing and improve deep graph convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search makes network design cheaper by replacing discrete architectural choices with continuously learned weights. However, DARTS can produce worse architectures as the search continues. This paper identifies a steep validation-loss landscape as an essential source of that instability, particularly when the continuous search result is converted into a final architecture.

The authors propose SmoothDARTS, which uses perturbation-based regularization to smooth that landscape. Two formulations apply either random smoothing or adversarial perturbations. Both aim to stabilize DARTS-based methods. The mathematical analysis shows that the method implicitly regularizes the norm of the validation-loss Hessian, connecting the perturbations to reduced curvature of the loss landscape.

Search trajectories on NAS-Bench-1Shot1 demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. Across different search spaces and four datasets, the improved stability also produces performance gains. The findings connect an identifiable source of search instability with a practical intervention and a mathematical explanation, addressing how well the continuously optimized search result translates into the architecture ultimately selected.
icml-2020-stabilizing-differentiable-arc.tldr: SmoothDARTS stabilizes differentiable architecture search by using perturbations to smooth validation loss and improve the selected architectures.

paragraphs: This paper studies how discrete stochastic update processes relate to a continuous stochastic differential equation. Its main results give quantitative rates for convergence to the equation’s invariant distribution, meaning a distribution that remains unchanged under its evolution. The focus is on Langevin-like processes and their connection to stochastic gradient methods.

The analysis allows additive noise to be non-Gaussian and to depend on the current state. It also permits a nonconvex potential function. Within this setting, the authors show that key properties depend on the potential and the noise’s second moment. This identifies features of the objective landscape and noise that matter for understanding the process.

The authors apply the theory to convergence of stochastic gradient descent on nonconvex problems. Experiments training deep neural networks on CIFAR-10 corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution links discrete optimization updates, their noise, and a continuous probabilistic description, providing quantitative convergence information for the analyzed processes and an application to neural-network training.
icml-2020-stochastic-gradient-and-langev.tldr: The paper proves distributional convergence rates for Langevin-like processes with flexible noise and applies the theory to nonconvex SGD.

paragraphs: Generative flows model probability distributions through invertible transformations, making density modeling tractable. That invertibility also constrains the architecture: intermediate representations must have the same dimensionality as the input data. This paper focuses on how the resulting restriction on network width can limit a flow’s expressiveness.

VFlow addresses the restriction by augmenting the data with additional dimensions. It jointly learns the distribution of the augmented data and a variational augmentation distribution through an evidence lower bound objective. The extra dimensions allow the model to work in a wider representation space while using a training objective designed for the augmented formulation.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that VFlow’s maximum-ELBO solution is always better than the original maximum-likelihood solution. That comparison is conditional on those assumptions and concerns the stated optimized objectives. For image density modeling on CIFAR-10, VFlow achieves 2.98 bits per dimension, reported as a new leading result. The theory and experiment support augmentation as a way to increase flow expressiveness.
icml-2020-vflow-more-expressive-generati.tldr: VFlow adds learned auxiliary dimensions to increase generative-flow expressiveness, with a conditional theoretical advantage and strong CIFAR-10 density modeling results.
